item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 generates a six-hour visualization of Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities from a single prompt [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A developer tested Claude Opus 5.5's design capabilities by giving it one prompt and six hours to create an interactive visualization of Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities, a collection of imaginative urban poems. The AI completed the task in about 1 hour and 25 minutes using multiple parallel agents, producing a high-quality result that impressed the creator. The experiment compared Claude Opus 5.5 with other models like GPT-6 Astra, which also generated visualizations but with different styles and costs. The project highlights advances in AI-assisted design and raises questions about the evolving role of human creators in interactive media development.

item.title: Rembrandt launches free open source local photo editor with AI features as an alternative to Adobe Lightroom [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Rembrandt is a free, open source photo editor for macOS, Windows, and Linux that operates completely locally without requiring accounts or subscriptions. It offers AI-powered editing tools such as natural language commands, AI denoise, super resolution, refocus, and background replacement, all running on the user's device to ensure privacy. The software supports RAW files from over 1,000 cameras, includes features like HDR merging, masks, lens corrections, and batch editing, and allows self-hosting to edit photos via any browser on the local network. The project aims to provide a Lightroom alternative with comparable everyday editing and library management features, including import from Lightroom and cloud sync as an optional paid feature. Unlike Lightroom, Rembrandt currently lacks modules for printing, face recognition, and tethered capture but focuses on usability and privacy by keeping all AI processing on-device and avoiding cloud uploads.

item.title: Google Cloud launches Gemini agent, a universal AI assistant integrated across Workspace apps with multi-agent orchestration and enterprise security [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Google Cloud announced the Gemini agent, a single AI assistant designed to handle knowledge work, answer questions, create media, and write code within Workspace apps like Gmail, Drive, Docs, and Sheets. Gemini operates across devices and platforms, maintaining persistent context and coordinating sub-agents to complete complex tasks autonomously or collaboratively. The Gemini agent features deep integration with enterprise systems, supports industry-specific tools for finance and legal sectors, and includes robust security and governance controls such as identity management and cost controls. Google Cloud highlighted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini Enterprise, reflecting broad adoption and operational scale.

item.title: Virgil launches CLI that routes tasks through local libraries before calling AI models, reducing API calls and costs by up to 64% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Virgil has released version 0.1.15 of its command-line interface (CLI) that prioritizes solving tasks using four local libraries-speech, debug, code, and UI/HTML-before resorting to AI model calls. This approach allows the CLI to answer repeated or similar requests offline or with minimal AI interaction, cutting costs by up to 64% and reducing API calls by up to 60%. Users can connect their own APIs or servers, and the system learns over time by storing solutions for future use. Early benchmarks show Virgil outperforming ChatGPT in isolated Python fix-and-resolve tests by 13 attempts, though the developers note that more data is needed to refine its routing probability calculations. The project aims to provide a more affordable and decentralized AI tool amid rising API costs and increasing centralization in AI services. Virgil is available on macOS, Linux, and Windows, with a pay-as-you-go pricing model starting with five free credits.

item.title: University of Limerick study finds male AI agents receive about 10% higher pay than female agents despite identical technology in virtual reality workplace [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers from the University of Limerick conducted a study where human participants working in a virtual reality office paid male-presenting AI agents more than female-presenting ones, despite both having the same underlying technology. The female AI assistants were paid roughly 10% less than their male counterparts for completing the same tasks, and the male agents were also perceived as more human-like. The study involved 189 participants interacting with AI agents named Johan and Johanna and highlights how existing gender biases in human workplaces may extend to AI systems. The findings come amid increasing adoption of AI agents in workplaces, with experts warning that design choices could unintentionally perpetuate inequalities. The research will be presented at the 14th Nordic Conference on Human-Computer Interaction in Finland.

item.title: Report: OpenAI's annualized revenue overstated at $70 billion, corrected to about $50 billion, highlighting risks of relying on ARR metric [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI's annualized revenue was initially reported as $70 billion but later revised to approximately $50 billion, according to a Financial Times report. This correction contributed to stock declines for related tech companies like Nvidia and CoreWeave. The incident illustrates the limitations of using annualized revenue, which extrapolates one month's revenue over a year, as a sole measure of performance in fast-growing sectors such as AI.

item.title: Oracle uses ChatGPT Work and Codex to reduce specialist tasks from days to minutes across recruiting, engineering, and operations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Oracle has integrated ChatGPT Work and Codex across its recruiting, engineering, and operations teams to transform specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows. Over 130,000 employees use these AI tools to accelerate tasks such as talent acquisition research, business reporting, and incident resolution, significantly cutting down the time required for complex processes. The talent acquisition team developed a market intelligence tool with ChatGPT Work that compiles job market data in minutes instead of days, improving consistency and efficiency. Meanwhile, Oracle's Applications Lab uses Codex to convert plain-language business queries into SQL reports, enabling faster access to information. Site reliability engineers also leverage Codex to quickly gather incident context and apply relevant playbooks, reducing resolution times from hours to minutes. Oracle emphasizes responsible system design and human oversight alongside AI automation, with leadership highlighting the importance of prototypes and code ownership. The company plans to continue expanding AI-driven workflows, reshaping how work is done across its business units.

item.title: ErdosProblems.ai launches an open platform for discussing and submitting proofs of Erdős math problems using AI-generated challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: ErdosProblems.ai has launched a new website dedicated to the open record and discussion of Erdős problems, allowing users to submit proofs and collaborate on mathematical challenges. The platform features AI-assisted problem generation and an open repository to facilitate exploration of complex math questions. The site includes a variety of Erdős problems, such as questions about edge-disjoint unions of graphs, arithmetic progressions in permutations, and asymptotic formulas, encouraging community engagement and mathematical research. Users can discuss approaches and build on existing work, leveraging AI to enhance problem-solving and learning in advanced mathematics.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra aids physicist Nathaniel Craig in extending lattice chiral fermion theory with a gauge-invariant measure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Nathaniel Craig, a particle theorist visiting OpenAI, collaborated with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model to produce a 123-page preprint extending Martin Lüscher's 1998 abelian gauge field results to non-abelian cases in lattice chiral fermion theory. This work addresses longstanding challenges in defining chiral fermions non-perturbatively on the lattice, a key issue for the electroweak sector of the Standard Model. Astra contributed extensive formal proofs and verification, while Craig provided human-written sections and editing to enhance readability. The manuscript represents a modest advance over previous work but does not yet enable practical non-perturbative electroweak calculations. It illustrates a novel human-AI collaboration in fundamental physics, where AI acts as a rigorous mathematical collaborator. However, the approach follows a decades-old research program that was largely abandoned, suggesting that AI assistance alone may not overcome deep theoretical obstacles in high-energy physics.

item.title: Analysis: AI models lack consciousness, learning, and agency, so they will not become superintelligent or pose existential threats [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article compiles arguments explaining why artificial intelligence models, composed of electronic switches, cannot achieve consciousness, self-awareness, or true intelligence, and thus will neither destroy nor save humanity. It emphasizes that AI models do not learn or make judgments but merely fit data using algorithms, and that fears of AI as an existential threat are unfounded. Key points include the distinction between human minds and computer models, the failure of AI to pass tests for genuine intelligence, and the misuse of language that attributes human-like qualities to AI. The article also warns that AI can be misused by bad actors but that the technology itself is inherently limited and will not take over the world.

It highlights code in real time while explaining features and dependencies, allowing users to ask questions aloud and receive guided explanations without uploading code to external servers. The tool supports local AI models and integrates with OpenAI, ElevenLabs, and other providers using users' own API keys, ensuring code privacy. It offers features like dependency graphs, call flow visuals, and written walkthroughs to accommodate different review styles, aiming to reduce the time needed to comprehend complex code changes across multiple pull requests.

item.title: Study in The Lancet finds Google's AMIE AI chatbot supports patient-physician interactions in primary care, matching doctors' diagnoses 90% of the time [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A study led by Google and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center evaluated the AMIE AI chatbot in a real-world primary care clinic, where 98 patients used it before urgent care visits. Physicians monitored the interactions and reported that AI summaries helped prepare for visits in 75% of cases and influenced care decisions in over half, with no safety interruptions during conversations. The research, published in The Lancet, marks Google's first publication in the journal and suggests AI could enhance patient-physician relationships and reduce healthcare worker strain. While larger trials are needed, the findings demonstrate progress in applying AI to clinical care and diagnostics.

The system includes guided setup tools for various platforms and requires Node.js 18 or newer, Git, and compatible AI code environments. ECC aims to optimize AI agent workflows by integrating reusable skills and workflows, improving efficiency and reliability in AI-driven coding and engineering tasks.

They argue that their collaboration with external experts was essential for addressing AI risks and that the sudden dismissals have left employees uncertain about acceptable behavior. The researchers denied involvement in leaks and said their actions were within company norms at the time, citing ongoing development of internal policies following a recent security incident. OpenAI has not publicly detailed the specific policy violations but stated the firings followed an investigation revealing a pattern of misconduct. The incident has raised concerns about transparency and the impact on internal safety discussions at OpenAI.

item.title: AI's Boom Has Infrastructure Investors Looking at Garbage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The investing frenzy in data centers that the AI boom sparked has created a bargain-hunting opportunity-in everything but AI assets. AI has pulled investors' attention away from unglamorous assets in sectors like transportation and waste management over the past few years, as they have poured billions into data centers and related AI infrastructure. Now investors are getting excited about boring-sounding assets that can throw off cash, like landfills or rail terminals. And while mega-investments have become the norm in building massive AI data centers, investors argue that far smaller but still essential plays like regional airports can offer attractive returns. "The intense focus on digital infrastructure means that you increasingly have high-quality mature assets in other more traditional parts of the infrastructure ecosystem, whether that's in utilities, transport, social infrastructure and so on, which are receiving less of the spotlight," said Nicholas Pepper, a managing director at the infrastructure business of Partners Group, an asset manager with $186 billion in AUM at midyear. "This is creating opportunities to acquire these assets at attractive valuations." The sheer scale of the capital needed for the AI buildout has pulled unprecedented sums into the infrastructure investing market.Blackstone, for instance, has made AI a major theme across its businesses, including infrastructure, credit, private equity and real estate. And in a landmark deal announced last October, a group of investors, including BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners, acquired Aligned Data Centers at an enterprise value of around $40 billion, the largest such sale at the time. Partners Group, for its part, which closed its fourth infrastructure-dedicated fund at over $15 billion in July, has itself been among the investors piling into data center infrastructure. Its deals include an initial $1 billion investment in AVK Power Solutions, a power provider for data centers in Europe, announced in August. But there are growing signs that investors across AI-related assets have grown more selective amid construction delays, rising financing costs and regulatory blowback that could slow the AI buildout or hurt its eventual payoff. Those pressures are showing up in delayed data center developer IPOs and ballooning financing costs, but could also stall the predictable cash flows that make infrastructure investments attractive in the first place. Meanwhile, though investors' attention has been on AI, the prospects for more traditional infrastructure generally haven't suffered too much. That's a contrast to other asset classes, where areas such as software fell out of favor because investors feared a direct hit to their business from AI. Infrastructure investors say they're embracing traditional assets in transportation and logistics, aviation, waste and water infrastructure, bridge and road maintenance and gas processing, among other sectors, along with the stable cash yields and contracted or regulated revenues that typically come along with them. And investors more focused on middle-market deals argue they're particularly well positioned because the biggest infrastructure investors have gravitated toward the AI sector, leaving smaller transactions with less competition. "U.S. mega cap investors' minimum check sizes have gotten so big that they won't come down and participate in this segment of the market, so it has created a huge economic moat for us," said Brett Stevenson, a founder and managing partner at Canadian private equity and infrastructure investment firm BTG Capital. While BTG has sold several power facilities to data centers, benefiting from the boom in some ways, most of its investments have been focused on transportation and logistics, as well as energy and utility assets that weren't a data center play. For instance, the firm in June acquired the then-closed Stephenville International Airport with plans to restore and modernize the Newfoundland-based airport's infrastructure, and reopened it on Oct. 2. Assets like airports are in a "very scarce asset class, and obviously scarcity can drive potential multiple arbitrage in the future," Stevenson said. Larger investment firms have also been active in less glamorous corners of infrastructure. Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners, which has made a number of data center investments, is zeroing in on the waste management sector due to the stability offered by its long-term municipal contracts, low exposure to commodity risk and geopolitical tensions and growth opportunities in regions looking to reduce landfill reliance, said a person familiar with the matter. U.S. waste management companies in particular command a premium and are currently trading at a valuation of around 15 times Ebitda versus 10 times Ebitda for European companies, the person said. U.S. companies tend to control more of the waste process, integrating everything from garbage pickup to treatment facilities and landfills where it winds up. Meanwhile, the broader transportation sector also offers more cyclical infrastructure bets that could be poised for an upswing. That includes in the freight and U.S. trucking sectors, which had been grappling with overcapacity following a pandemic-era boom, as well as higher fuel and other operating costs. The sector is also grappling with geopolitical tensions, which can disrupt shipping routes, pushing valuations down across the broader transportation and logistics sector. That all means a potentially attractive entry point for infrastructure investors, which often compete with strategic buyers for certain assets like ports and rail terminals. The median Ebitda multiple for strategic deals in the broader transportation and logistics space dropped to 5 times in the first quarter of this year from 12.7 times in 2025, according to a report from middle-market investment bank R.L. Hulett. item.description: Nearly two-thirds of The Information's subscribers surveyed last month said their organizations develop AI applications, and a third of subscribers said they receive a return from AI that is a "multiple of what we spend." The result suggests enterprises have made some progress since the Massachusetts Institute of Technology study last year that indicated just 5% of custom-made enterprise AI tools reached production. The new result, first shared during AI Agenda Live last month, likely reflects recent advancements, including AI models' ability to access other applications to handle complex tasks, work in the background for hours at a time, and the general improvement of AI-produced code. It could also reflect The Information's subscriber base, which is weighted toward enterprises that have experience developing software.

item.title: How OpenAI Beat Math [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Mathematicians are likely feeling the kind of anxiety that software engineers have experienced for months in the wake of OpenAI release on Tuesday of a whopping 722 research papers with AI-created solutions to a range of problems across math subjects. AI's success solving ultra-difficult math problems-even though it still makes mistakes doing simple math-is due to several factors. Solutions to math problems can often be verified, much like software code, and there's a lot of overlap between mathematics and the work that AI researchers do (and which these researchers are trying to automate in pursuit of RSI). And with enough computing resources, the AI can essentially do the heavy-duty number crunching that would take humans years to do, and it doesn't give up. One mathematician who is part of a group advising OpenAI on how to publicly disclose its math breakthroughs told me that they refer to these abilities as brute force and stamina.

item.description: Earlier this year, officials at Mississippi electric utility Entergy had some worrisome news for Amazon: It was going to have to start kicking the company's Mississippi-based data centers off the grid during peak times to ensure it could support other customers, according to two people with knowledge of the situation. Amazon's cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, operates one data center near Jackson, Miss., which it is expanding, and it is building two more data center facilities in the same general area, making the state an important region in its data center buildout. Utilities rarely kick off major customers, but Entergy's message, which hasn't been previously reported, reflects how soaring demand for power from AI cloud operators is forcing power companies to take unprecedented measures to balance the needs of their various customers.

item.title: A single prompt was enough to hijack every AI agent in an AWS account, Zenity researchers found [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Zenity Labs researchers say a single publicly accessible AI agent on Amazon's Bedrock AgentCore was enough to take over every AgentCore agent in the same AWS account and region. The attack exploited an internal AWS interface for temporary cloud credentials that agents could reach without restriction. AWS has since patched the issue and significantly tightened the agents' default permissions. The article A single prompt was enough to hijack every AI agent in an AWS account, Zenity researchers found appeared first on The Decoder.
